title: Yamauba blackening Her teeth and Kintoki

source.label: Binyon and Sexton (1923): the Yama-uba series, “at the very end of the century”
Wikipedia: “Ukiyo-e of yama-uba with blackened teeth and Kintarō”

work.text: In the sets of prints illustrating that favourite subject of his, the life of the strong boy Kintoki and his wild mother of the mountains, Utamaro is at his most original, soars highest above the common world
Utamaro created as many as 50 designs depicting the intimate relationship between mother and child.

moment.text: He struck away from the world of Ukiyo-ye into the world of legend ; and he chose the story of the savage mountain-fairy who fostered and brought up in the wilds with a more than mother's devotion

source.author: Laurence Binyon and J. J. O'Brien Sexton

moment.text: In Japanese mythology, Yamauba is typically shown as a witch, but here Kitagawa Utamaro transformed her into a beautiful woman. She cares for her infant son, the legendary strong boy Kintarō.

matters.text: Here was the maternal passion isolated and removed from all the dainty and delicate refinements of a city-life and home ; just the primitive, jealous, animal intensity of that love ; this alone could satisfy Utamaro's imagination.

matters.text: Utamaro was married although little is known about his wife and there is no record of their having had children. However, his works include many prints of tender and intimate domestic scenes featuring the same woman and child over several years.
